about: References written inside prose. In a knowledge base most of the graph lives in the writing rather than in the schema, and a format that only models declared reference fields cannot see it. The rule is that prose stays opaque and its edges are mirrored into relations, so a consumer that cannot read your dialect can still hold your graph — and knows what it is about to break.

cases.why: A tool with no prose at all still has to come out of this holding the edge. Mirroring inline references into relations is what makes that possible: the link between two notes is a fact about the library, and locking it inside one producer's markup dialect makes it a fact only that producer can read.

cases.why: Nobody has to understand double brackets, double parens, or whatever the next tool invents. The format deliberately does not standardise a markup dialect — it standardises that yours comes back exactly as you wrote it. A consumer that normalises prose into its own syntax has rewritten the user's writing, which is the one thing in a knowledge base nobody wants touched.

This is what the mirror buys. A tool that rewrites prose into its own markup cannot know whether it just destroyed a link, because it cannot parse the dialect it is replacing — but the relations array told it there was one. Without the mirror the loss is not merely unreported, it is undetectable.

A mention whose target has been deleted is not noise to be tidied away. It is the only remaining record that the writing points at something, and it is what lets a tool offer to fix or clear the link rather than leaving a reader to wonder what the sentence meant. Dropping an edge because its far end is missing quietly rewrites the prose's meaning.

A tool with only untyped backlinks must keep the type, and must keep where the edge came from. Flattening an inline mention and a declared reference field into the same undifferentiated link loses the difference between what someone wrote in a sentence and what they filled into a form, and only one of those can be edited without touching the prose.

The mirror is only trustworthy if it points at something real. An edge claiming to come from a field the type does not have is either a stale export or a producer guessing, and a consumer has no way to tell which — so it is caught here rather than becoming a link nobody can trace back to a sentence.

A mention with no id is a bare row unless it says what it said. Without the label a consumer cannot render the sentence around it — the reader is left with prose that plainly refers to somebody and no way to know who — and cannot offer to create the missing thing or clear the link. The label is the whole difference between a broken reference and a reference to something that does not exist yet.

`to` may be absent — a mention of a person who does not exist yet is a normal thing to write, and it has a name and no id. What is not allowed is neither: an edge with no id and no label points at nothing and says nothing, and a consumer can do exactly nothing with it except carry it forever.
